steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on PreLoad, a method that keeps point-estimated discriminative neural networks from being arbitrarily confident on data far from the training set. Cover the overconfidence problem, why existing calibration, OOD-detection, generative and Bayesian approaches fall short, and what our method does.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Context: ML progress, safety-critical deployment, uncertainty quantification expectations
- DNN overconfidence (in-domain and far away; ReLU networks)
- Existing remedies: calibration, Bayesian / non-Bayesian OOD detection
- OOD training with extra data and its limits
- Generative modeling and Bayesian neural networks
- PreLoad: desiderata and construction
- Figure 1 comparison

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Context
  - ML progress over last decade: deep learning toolkit, larger data sets, better optimization, faster/cheaper computation, vibrant community
  - deployment in safety-critical applications -> questions about robustness, uncertainty quantification
  - expectation: high confidence near training data, low confidence on out-of-distribution (OOD) test cases
- DNN overconfidence
  - DNNs: powerful function approximators, part of recent advances
  - overconfident in-domain (cite) and far away from training examples (cite)
  - prior work (cite): ReLU networks almost always highly confident far from training data
- Existing remedies
  - calibration: smoothing softmax distribution (cite), regularization (cite), extra loss constraints (cite)
  - do not resolve overconfidence around OOD data (cite)
  - Bayesian (cite) and non-Bayesian (cite) methods improve OOD detection training only on in-domain data
- OOD training with extra data
  - SOTA OOD detection: extra OOD training data; classifier outputs high "None" class probability (cite) or uniform confidence (cite)
  - prior work (cite): no guarantee OOD data predicted as "None"
  - we show: still high confidence far away from data
- Generative modeling / Bayesian NNs
  - generative modeling in NN: posthoc (cite) or as prior on data (cite)
  - posthoc: assumes embedding ~ Gaussian; not competitive with SOTA on realistic OOD data
  - prior on data: generative model over data, harder than discriminative modeling
  - Bayesian neural networks (cite): no guarantee of optimal confidences on far-away OOD data (cite)
  - more sophisticated remedy (cite): built only to fix far-away high confidence; nearby OOD detection an afterthought
- PreLoad
  - Producing Larger Logits away from Data
  - desiderata: (i) keep simplicity of standard discriminative training (unlike generative/Bayesian), (ii) provably less confident far from training data, (iii) good on realistic OOD (CIFAR-10 vs. CIFAR-100)
  - train an extra class; extra logit larger than others for OOD input as we move away from data
  - provably: almost always predicts far-away data as OOD
  - extra class trained on auxiliary OOD dataset -> detects realistic nearby OOD
- Figure 1
  - confidence of PreLoad moving away from data vs standard network and Outlier Exposure (cite)
  - standard softmax nets: high confidence away from decision boundary
  - OE: confidence first decreases, then high far away when zooming out
  - PreLoad: confident near data, uncertain away

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Over the last decade machine learning has made a lot of progress, helped by a strong deep learning toolkit, larger data sets, better optimization algorithms, faster and cheaper computation, and a vibrant research community. Machine learning systems keep being deployed in safety-critical applications, so people keep asking important questions about their robustness and uncertainty quantification. In uncertainty quantification it is commonly expected that test cases close to the training data get high confidence and test cases that are out-of-distribution (OOD) get low confidence.

Part of the recent advances in machine learning come from deep neural networks (DNNs), which are powerful function approximators. But DNN classifiers tend to be overconfident, both for in-domain examples and for data far away from the training examples. Prior work showed that ReLU Networks, which are used everywhere, almost always show high confidence on samples far away from the training data.

Many methods have been proposed for the overconfidence issue in DNNs. Calibration methods try to fix the overconfidence of neural network classifiers in several ways, such as smoothing the softmax distribution, regularization and adding more constraints to the loss function. But these methods do not solve the overconfidence issues around OOD data. Other methods, both Bayesian and non-Bayesian, have improved OOD detection while training only with the in-domain data distribution.

The state-of-the-art methods for OOD detection are usually trained with additional OOD training data, so that the classifier outputs either a high "None" class probability or uniform confidence when there are OOD samples. The same work showed that there is no guarantee that OOD data would be predicted as the "None" class. We will also show that these methods are still highly confident when the test points are far away from the data.

- Generative modeling / Bayesian NNs
  - generative modeling in NN: posthoc or as prior on data
  - posthoc: embedding ~ Gaussian; not competitive with SOTA on realistic OOD data
  - prior on data: harder than discriminative modeling
  - Bayesian neural networks: no guarantee of optimal confidences far away
  - more sophisticated remedy: only fixes far-away high confidence; nearby OOD an afterthought
- PreLoad (Producing Larger Logits away from Data)
  - desiderata: (i) simple standard discriminative training, (ii) provably less confident far away, (iii) good on realistic OOD (CIFAR-10 vs. CIFAR-100)
  - extra class whose logit grows larger than others away from data -> provably far-away data almost always OOD
  - extra class trained on auxiliary OOD dataset -> nearby OOD
- Figure 1: PreLoad vs standard network vs Outlier Exposure
  - standard: high confidence away from decision boundary
  - OE: decreases first, high far away when zooming out
  - PreLoad: confident near data, uncertain away

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Over the last decade machine learning has made a lot of progress, helped by a strong deep learning toolkit, larger data sets, better optimization algorithms, faster and cheaper computation, and a vibrant research community. Machine learning systems keep being deployed in safety-critical applications, so people keep asking important questions about their robustness and uncertainty quantification. In uncertainty quantification it is commonly expected that test cases close to the training data get high confidence and test cases that are out-of-distribution (OOD) get low confidence.

Part of the recent advances in machine learning come from deep neural networks (DNNs), which are powerful function approximators. But DNN classifiers tend to be overconfident, both for in-domain examples and for data far away from the training examples. Prior work showed that ReLU Networks, which are used everywhere, almost always show high confidence on samples far away from the training data.

Many methods have been proposed for the overconfidence issue in DNNs. Calibration methods try to fix the overconfidence of neural network classifiers in several ways, such as smoothing the softmax distribution, regularization and adding more constraints to the loss function. But these methods do not solve the overconfidence issues around OOD data. Other methods, both Bayesian and non-Bayesian, have improved OOD detection while training only with the in-domain data distribution.

The state-of-the-art methods for OOD detection are usually trained with additional OOD training data, so that the classifier outputs either a high "None" class probability or uniform confidence when there are OOD samples. The same work showed that there is no guarantee that OOD data would be predicted as the "None" class. We will also show that these methods are still highly confident when the test points are far away from the data.

One way to get around arbitrarily high confidence on far-away data is to put generative modeling into a neural network, either as a posthoc method or as a prior on the data. The posthoc methods assume that the neural network embedding can be approximated with a Gaussian distribution. But we will show that on realistic OOD data these methods are not competitive with the state-of-the-art. The prior-on-data approach assumes a generative model over the data, and this is a harder problem than the discriminative modeling underneath.

Lastly, Bayesian neural networks have also been used for this issue, but they are not guaranteed to get the optimal confidences on far-away OOD test data. There is a more sophisticated remedy for this, but it is constructed specifically to fix only the far-away high confidence, and its detection performance on 'nearby' OOD data is more of an afterthought.

In this work we present our method, Producing Larger Logits away from Data, or PreLoad, which meets these desiderata: (i) it must keep the simplicity of the standard discriminative training procedure for DNNs (unlike methods based on generative models and Bayesian methods), (ii) it must provably be less confident on inputs far away from the training data, and (iii) it must do well on realistic OOD examples (e.g. CIFAR-10 vs. CIFAR-100).

We do this by training an extra class, so that for an OOD input this extra logit becomes larger than the logits of the other classes as we move farther from the training data. With this construction PreLoad provably almost always predicts far-away data as OOD. Also, the extra class is trained on an auxiliary OOD dataset, and this helps it to detect realistic, nearby OOD examples well.

Figure 1 shows the confidence level of PreLoad as we move away from the training data, compared to a standard-trained neural network and to a discriminative OOD training approach called Outlier Exposure. Standard neural networks with a softmax output layer are highly confident as we move away from the decision boundary. The confidence of OE first decreases away from the data, but becomes high far away when we zoom out. PreLoad on the other hand is confident close to the data and uncertain away from it.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Machine learning has made substantial progress over the last decade, thanks to a strong deep learning toolkit, larger data sets, better optimization algorithms, faster and cheaper computation, and a vibrant research community. As machine learning systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, important questions about their robustness and uncertainty quantification continue to be asked. A common expectation in uncertainty quantification is that test cases close to the training data receive high confidence and test cases that are out-of-distribution (OOD) receive low confidence.

Recent advances in machine learning are partly due to deep neural networks (DNNs), which are powerful function approximators. However, DNN classifiers tend to be overconfident both for in-domain examples [1] and for data far away from the training examples [2]. [3] showed that the ubiquitous ReLU Networks almost always exhibit high confidence on samples far away from the training data.

A number of methods have been proposed to deal with overconfidence in DNNs. Calibration methods try to address the overconfidence of neural network classifiers through various means, including smoothing the softmax distribution [1,4,5], regularization [6,7] and adding constraints to the loss function [8,9]. These methods, however, do not resolve overconfidence around OOD data [10]. Other methods, both Bayesian [11,12,13] and non-Bayesian [14,15], have improved OOD detection while training only on the in-domain data distribution.

State-of-the-art methods for OOD detection are typically trained with additional OOD training data so that, in the presence of OOD samples, the classifier outputs either a high "None" class probability [16,17] or uniform confidence [18]. [3] showed that there is no guarantee that OOD data would be predicted as the "None" class. Moreover, we will demonstrate that these methods still exhibit high confidence when test points are far away from the data.

One way to overcome arbitrarily high confidence on far-away data is to incorporate generative modeling into a neural network, either as a posthoc method [19,15] or as a prior on the data [20]. The former assumes that the neural network embedding can be approximated by a Gaussian distribution; however, we will demonstrate that on realistic OOD data these methods are not competitive with the state-of-the-art. The latter assumes a generative model over the data, which is a harder problem than the underlying discriminative modeling.

Finally, while Bayesian neural networks [21,22] have also been used to address this issue, they are not guaranteed to obtain the optimal confidences on far-away OOD test data [13]. A more sophisticated remedy exists [23], but it is specifically constructed to fix only the far-away high confidence, and its detection performance on 'nearby' OOD data is more of an afterthought.

In this work, we present our method, Producing Larger Logits away from Data, or PreLoad, which fulfills the following desiderata: (i) it must maintain the simplicity of the standard discriminative training procedure for DNNs (unlike generative- and Bayesian-based methods), (ii) it must provably be less confident on inputs far away from the training data, and (iii) it must perform well on realistic OOD examples (e.g. CIFAR-10 vs. CIFAR-100).

We achieve this by training an extra class such that, for an OOD input, the extra logit becomes larger than the logits of the other classes as we move farther away from the training data. This construction provably makes PreLoad almost always predict far-away data as OOD. Furthermore, the extra class is trained on an auxiliary OOD dataset, which helps it detect realistic, nearby OOD examples well.

Figure 1 illustrates the confidence of PreLoad as we move away from the training data, compared to a standard-trained neural network and to a discriminative OOD training approach called Outlier Exposure [18]. Standard neural networks with a softmax output layer exhibit high confidence as we move away from the decision boundary. OE's confidence initially decreases away from the data but becomes high far away as we zoom out. In contrast, PreLoad is confident close to the data and uncertain away from it.
